chunks: "Both rely on the fact that current makes a magnetic field and a magnetic field pushes on current. A solenoid is a coil with a movable iron plunger.
When you drive current through the coil, it creates a magnetic field, and the iron gets pulled in toward where the field is strongest, which closes the air gap.
A spring pulls the plunger back out when the current stops. The force is strongest when the gap is small, and it goes up with the square of the current times turns.
A brushed DC motor has a coil on the rotor sitting between magnets on the stator.
Current in the coil in that magnetic field gives a force on each side of the loop, F equals B I L, in opposite directions, so you get a torque.
After half a turn the forces would reverse, so the commutator and brushes flip the current direction in the coil, and the torque keeps pushing the same way.
Torque is proportional to current: tau equals K t times I.
The second half of the story is that a coil moving through a field generates a voltage, the back-EMF, proportional to speed, and it opposes the supply.
So as the motor speeds up, the net voltage across the resistance falls and the current drops. That's why a motor draws a big current at start and a small one at full speed."
